opus-5.5.text:
I think it really depends on what stage you're at and what problem you're actually trying to solve. My honest view is that for most robot learning companies right now, the bottleneck isn't the hardware itself — it's data, and how fast you can iterate on the learning side. So if there's existing hardware that's good enough, I'd lean toward using it and putting your energy into the models and the data pipeline.

But there's a catch. A lot of the off-the-shelf hardware wasn't designed with learning in mind. Industrial arms were built for precise, repeatable motion in structured settings: high stiffness, position control, very expensive, not really meant to make contact with the world in messy ways. Learning-based approaches often want something different: lower cost so you can build many units and collect a lot of data, more compliance and safety so the robot can touch things and fail without breaking itself or hurting people, and good sensing in the right places, like wrist cameras or tactile sensing. When the available hardware doesn't match those needs, you end up fighting it, and that's when building your own starts to make sense.

There's also a co-design argument. The hardware determines what data you can collect, and the data determines what the model can learn. If you control both, you can make choices like simplifying the gripper, or designing the teleoperation interface so the human demonstrations map cleanly onto what the robot can do. Those small decisions compound a lot. Some of the most effective systems I've seen came from people who were willing to make the hardware a bit "worse" by traditional standards — less precise, cheaper — because it made data collection much easier and the learning handled the rest.

That said, hardware is hard, slow, and capital-intensive. Every hardware iteration costs months, while a model iteration might take days. So my rough rule of thumb: don't build hardware for its own sake. Build it when you've clearly identified that the hardware is the limiting factor for your data or your deployment, and keep it as simple as possible. Ideally it should be something other people can reproduce, because the more people collecting data on similar platforms, the faster the whole field moves.

r001.rationale: The response explains that off-the-shelf hardware may not meet learning needs such as low cost, compliance, safety, and suitable sensing, and that building custom hardware makes sense when available systems do not match the application.

fable-5.1.text:
This is a question I get asked a lot, and my honest answer is: it depends on what you believe the bottleneck is.

If you think the bottleneck is data, then the hardware question becomes a data question. Every time you change the embodiment — the gripper, the arm length, the camera placement — you create a distribution shift. Data collected on one body doesn't transfer cleanly to another. So companies that design their own hardware are really making a bet that they can control the embodiment well enough to keep their data consistent over years, not months. That's a very expensive bet, because hardware iteration is slow, and if you get the morphology wrong early, all the data you collected on that morphology loses value.

On the other hand, if you rely on third-party hardware, you inherit someone else's decisions. The sensors might not be what you want, the latency in the control loop might be bad, the hands might be designed for teleoperation rather than for learning. And those constraints quietly shape what your model can and cannot learn. I've seen teams spend six months working around a hardware limitation that would have been a two-week fix if they owned the design.

So my view is somewhere in the middle. You don't need to build everything. You probably shouldn't build your own actuators or motors — that's a decade-long discipline with its own supply chain. But you probably do need to own the parts of the hardware that touch the data most directly: the end effector, the sensing, the control interface. Those are the places where a learning company has a different opinion from a traditional robotics company, and that opinion needs to be expressed in hardware.

The other thing I'd say is that the answer changes depending on the stage. Early on, buy whatever lets you collect data fastest and learn what matters. Once you know what matters, that's when custom hardware starts paying for itself. A lot of companies get this backwards — they build beautiful hardware before they know what the model actually needs, and then they're locked in.

r001.rationale: The response explains that third-party hardware may have unsuitable sensors, control latency, or hands, and recommends custom hardware for components that directly affect learning data. This communicates that available systems may not fit the intended application.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you need to learn. In robotics, the hardware determines what you can observe, what actions you can take, and what data you can collect. So it’s difficult to treat the machine-learning system as completely separate from the physical platform.

But that doesn’t mean every robotics company should design its own hardware from scratch. If an existing platform gives you the sensing, reliability, and control you need, using it lets you focus on learning. Building hardware adds manufacturing, maintenance, and a much slower iteration cycle.

The reason to build your own is when the hardware is a bottleneck to the capability you’re trying to achieve. Maybe you need a different gripper, a different sensor placement, or better access to the control loop. Then owning that part of the design can make sense.

So I would start with the task and work backward: what does the robot need to do, what is preventing it from doing that, and does solving that problem actually require custom hardware?

r001.rationale: The response says custom hardware can make sense when hardware limits a desired capability, but it does not state that no commercially available system fits the intended application.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on whether the hardware is limiting what you’re trying to learn. You don’t necessarily need to design a robot from scratch, but you do need enough control over the hardware to get good data and reliably execute what the model predicts.

In robotics, the hardware and the learning system are closely connected. Where you put the cameras, what the gripper can do, how precisely you can control the motion—all of that affects what the model can learn. If an existing platform meets those needs, I’d use it. Designing your own hardware adds a lot of work.

But if you’re constantly working around limitations in sensing, control, or reliability, then building some of that hardware yourself can make sense. The goal is to own the parts that matter for your learning loop, rather than assume you have to own the entire robot.

r001.rationale: The response says to use an existing platform if it meets the learning needs, but to build hardware when existing platforms impose sensing, control, or reliability limitations. This communicates that a suitable off-the-shelf system may not fit the application.
